pos: v.t. & v.i. (to fail of hitting; to perceive the absence of)
etymology: Old English missan, to fail to hit. The Authorized Version uses both senses, and the second — to miss a person, to notice a seat is empty — carries one of the most affecting scenes in the friendship of David and Jonathan.
biblical_def: The first sense is marksmanship, and it produces one of Scripture's most startling statistics: among Benjamin there were “seven hundred chosen men lefthanded; every one could sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss” (Judges 20:16). The second sense is relational and it governs 1 Samuel 20. David asks Jonathan to cover for him: “If thy father at all miss me, then say, David earnestly asked leave of me that he might run to Bethlehem his city” (1 Samuel 20:6), and Jonathan answers with the sentence that sets the whole test: “To morrow is the new moon: and thou shalt be missed, because thy seat will be empty” (1 Samuel 20:18). An empty seat at a feast is what exposed Saul's murderous intent. The word can also mean simply gone: David's men had protected Nabal's shepherds so that “neither was there ought missing unto them, all the while they were in Carmel” (1 Samuel 25:7). To miss, in Scripture, is to register an absence — of a mark, of a man, of a thing entrusted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines miss as to fail of reaching or hitting; to fail of obtaining; and also, to perceive the want of, to discover something to be lost.
webster_full: MISS, v.t. To fail of hitting, reaching, finding or obtaining; as, to miss the mark.
MISS, v.t. To discover to be unexpectedly wanting; to perceive the want of; as, I missed my purse.
MISS, v.i. To fail to hit; to fly wide; to deviate from the true direction.
MISS, n. Loss; want; as, the miss of a friend; also, mistake; error.
ABSENCE, n. A state of being at a distance in place; the want or non-existence of a thing in a place.
scriptures: Judges 20:16
Among all this people there were seven hundred chosen men lefthanded; every one could sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss.
1 Samuel 20:6
If thy father at all miss me, then say, David earnestly asked leave of me that he might run to Bethlehem his city: for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the family.
1 Samuel 20:18
Then Jonathan said to David, To morrow is the new moon: and thou shalt be missed, because thy seat will be empty.
1 Samuel 25:7
And now I have heard that thou hast shearers: now thy shepherds which were with us, we hurt them not, neither was there ought missing unto them, all the while they were in Carmel.
corruption_summary: Absence is easily treated as neutral, a matter of private convenience, where Scripture makes the empty seat evidence — of a friendship, of a danger, and of where a man's allegiance actually lies.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation is to think that absence costs nothing and signifies nothing — that a place unfilled at a table, a gathering or a Lord's Day assembly is a private matter with no message in it. 1 Samuel 20:18 assumes the opposite as a matter of course: thou shalt be missed, because thy seat will be empty. Jonathan does not have to explain why an empty seat will be noticed; in a household, a covenant or a congregation it always is. The whole plot of the chapter turns on the fact that being missed is inevitable and revealing.

The other sense supplies the sharper warning. The Hebrew for sin is built on the idea of missing a mark, and Judges 20:16 gives the picture in its clearest form: seven hundred men who could sling at a hair breadth and not miss. Precision is possible, the target is real, and failure to hit it is failure however sincere the throw. That is exactly what Scripture means by sin — not merely bad intent but an actual missing of the glory of God — and it is why the remedy has to be an imputed righteousness rather than a better aim.
roots_summary: Hebrew chata (H2398), to miss the mark, hence to sin; paqad (H6485), to visit, to miss or muster; req (H7387), empty; adar (H5737), to be lacking.
roots_lines: Hebrew chata (H2398) — to miss the mark; the same root that gives the Hebrew word for sin.
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, to number, to miss; if thy father at all miss me.
Hebrew req (H7387) — empty, vain; thy seat will be empty.
Hebrew adar (H5737) — to be lacking, to fail; neither was there ought missing unto them.
Greek hamartano (G264) — to miss the mark, to err, to sin; all have sinned and come short.
usage: “Could sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss” — the mark is real.
“Thou shalt be missed, because thy seat will be empty” — absence speaks.
“Neither was there ought missing unto them” — a trust honestly kept.

pos: v.t. (to wait for; to look for as about to come)
etymology: Latin exspectare, to look out for, from ex and spectare, to look. The Authorized Version's most famous use is the expected end of Jeremiah 29, and its most solemn is the Son at God's right hand, expecting.
biblical_def: To a people just carried into Babylon, and told to build houses and plant gardens there, God says: “For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end” (Jeremiah 29:11). The promise is made to exiles with seventy years to serve, and the end in view is God's, not theirs. The New Testament sets the word twice against each other. At the Beautiful gate the lame man “gave heed unto them, expecting to receive something of them” (Acts 3:5) — he expected alms and received his feet. And of Christ enthroned: “From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool” (Hebrews 10:13). The Son, having offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down, and what he does now is expect. Christian waiting is patterned on that: not the nervous hope that something may turn out, but the settled expectation of a thing already secured and certainly coming.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines expect as to wait for; to look for as about to happen; to have a previous apprehension of something future, whether good or evil.
webster_full: EXPECT, v.t. To wait for; to look for as about to happen or come.
EXPECT, v.t. To look for with some confidence; to have a previous apprehension of something future.
EXPECTATION, n. The act of expecting or looking forward to a future event with at least some reason to believe it will happen.
HOPE, n. A desire of some good, accompanied with at least a slight expectation of obtaining it.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
scriptures: Jeremiah 29:11
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
Acts 3:5
And he gave heed unto them, expecting to receive something of them.
Hebrews 10:13
From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool.
Jeremiah 29:10
For thus saith the LORD, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.
corruption_summary: Jeremiah 29:11 is quoted as a personal guarantee of comfortable outcomes, stripped of the seventy years of captivity it was given inside and of the corporate exiles it was addressed to.
corruption_paragraphs: No verse in Scripture is more often lifted from its setting. Jeremiah 29:11 appears on cards and walls as a pledge that God intends pleasant things for the reader in the near term. The verse before it fixes the actual terms: That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place. The promise is corporate, it is covenantal, and nearly every adult who first heard it died in Babylon. It is not less comforting for that — it is far more, because it is a promise that survives the grave of the generation that received it — but it is not a guarantee of a smooth year.

Hebrews 10:13 teaches the right posture. Christ is not anxious about the outcome; he has offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, he has sat down, and he expects. His enemies shall be made his footstool, and the waiting is confident because the work is finished. Acts 3 shows what such expectation meets: a man expecting coins and receiving the use of his legs. God's expected end is regularly larger than the one we were looking out for, which is exactly why the promise is worth more than our version of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew tiqvah (H8615), a cord, hence hope or expectation; acharith (H319), the latter end; Greek prosdokao (G4328), to look for; ekdechomai (G1551), to wait for.
roots_lines: Hebrew tiqvah (H8615) — a cord, and so a thing hoped for; the expected end of Jeremiah 29:11.
Hebrew acharith (H319) — the after-part, the latter end; what God gives rather than what we plan.
Hebrew machashabah (H4284) — a thought, a purpose; the thoughts God thinks toward his people.
Greek prosdokao (G4328) — to watch toward, to expect; the lame man at the Beautiful gate.
Greek ekdechomai (G1551) — to wait for, to expect; the enthroned Christ of Hebrews 10:13.
usage: “Thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end”.
“Expecting to receive something of them” — and receiving far more.
“From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool”.

pos: v.i. (to come to a place, especially by water)
etymology: Late Latin arripare, to come to shore, from ad ripam, to the bank. The original sense is nautical, and the Authorized Version keeps it: both occurrences are landings after a voyage.
biblical_def: Luke, who wrote both passages, uses the word with a sailor's precision. After the storm on the lake, “they arrived at the country of the Gadarenes, which is over against Galilee” (Luke 8:26) — and the landing party met the man with the legion. In the travel diary of the third missionary journey the word marks one port among several: “And we sailed thence, and came the next day over against Chios; and the next day we arrived at Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; and the next day we came to Miletus” (Acts 20:15). The plainness is the point. Luke was there, he kept the log, and the gospel moved across the Aegean in named stages on ordinary ships. Scripture's arrivals are not vague; they are dated, they are located, and they can be checked. The faith rests on events that happened at particular harbours on particular days.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines arrive as to come to; to reach; to come to or reach by water or by travelling; and hence, to gain or compass by effort.
webster_full: ARRIVE, v.i. To come to; to reach in progress by water, originally; now used also of coming by land.
ARRIVE, v.i. To reach a point by progressive motion; to gain or compass by effort, practice or study.
ARRIVE, v.i. To happen or occur; as, the event arrived at the expected time.
VOYAGE, n. A passing by sea or water from one place, port or country to another.
HARBOR, n. A port or haven for ships; a lodging for the night; a place of safety.
scriptures: Luke 8:26
And they arrived at the country of the Gadarenes, which is over against Galilee.
Acts 20:15
And we sailed thence, and came the next day over against Chios; and the next day we arrived at Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; and the next day we came to Miletus.
Luke 8:27
And when he went forth to land, there met him out of the city a certain man, which had devils long time, and ware no clothes, neither abode in any house, but in the tombs.
Acts 20:16
For Paul had determined to sail by Ephesus, because he would not spend the time in Asia: for he hasted, if it were possible for him, to be at Jerusalem the day of Pentecost.
corruption_summary: The gospel narratives are often treated as timeless religious stories whose geography is decorative; Luke wrote them as a traveller with a log, naming ports a reader could visit.
corruption_paragraphs: A persistent way of handling the gospels and Acts is to treat their value as symbolic and their detail as ornament: what matters is the meaning, and the ports, provinces and dates are local colour. Acts 20:15 is a hard verse for that approach. Chios, Samos, Trogyllium, Miletus, each with the interval between them noted, written by a man using the word we. No one inventing a religion writes a sailing itinerary. The Christian faith is not a set of timeless truths illustrated by stories; it is the report of things that happened, and the report keeps a log.

Luke 8:26 shows what the precision is for. They arrived at a real country, over against Galilee, and there they met a man whose name was Legion. The demoniac, the swine, the terrified townsfolk asking Jesus to depart, and the healed man sent home to publish what great things God had done — all of it happens at a landing place. The recovery is a robust historical confidence: our Lord's power over devils was exercised at an address, on a day, in front of witnesses who counted the pigs.
roots_summary: Greek katapleo (G2668), to sail down to land; paraballo (G3846), to arrive alongside; ploos (G4144), a voyage; limen (G3040), a harbour.
roots_lines: Greek katapleo (G2668) — to sail down, to put in to shore; they arrived at the country of the Gadarenes.
Greek paraballo (G3846) — to throw alongside, to arrive at; we arrived at Samos.
Greek ploos (G4144) — a voyage, a sailing; the setting of Luke's we-passages.
Greek limen (G3040) — a harbour; the named ports of Acts 20 and 27.
Greek legion (G3003) — a legion; the name given at the landing in Luke 8.
usage: “They arrived at the country of the Gadarenes” — a real shore.
“The next day we arrived at Samos” — a log, not a legend.
“And tarried at Trogyllium” — detail no myth-maker supplies.

pos: n. (the act of asking; a search for information)
etymology: Old French enquerre, from Latin inquirere, to seek into. The Authorized Version spells it with an e, and uses it twice — once as a warning about enquiry made too late, and once as the plain work of finding a house in Joppa.
biblical_def: Proverbs sets the word in a proverb about rash religion: “It is a snare to the man who devoureth that which is holy, and after vows to make enquiry” (Proverbs 20:25). The order is the whole point. A man consecrates something, or swears something, and only afterwards begins to ask what he has committed himself to — and the proverb calls that a snare. Enquiry belongs before the vow. The second use is entirely practical and sits at the hinge of the book of Acts: while Peter was on the housetop puzzling over his vision, “behold, the men which were sent from Cornelius had made enquiry for Simon's house, and stood before the gate” (Acts 10:17). Three men asking directions in a strange town are, at that moment, the instrument by which the gospel goes to the Gentiles. God's providence commonly arrives as somebody at the gate who has been asking the way.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines enquiry as the act of asking for information; a question; and search for truth, information or knowledge.
webster_full: ENQUIRY, n. The act of inquiring; a seeking for information by asking questions; interrogation.
ENQUIRY, n. Search for truth, information or knowledge; examination into facts or principles.
ENQUIRE, v.i. To ask a question; to seek for truth or information by asking questions.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God; a promise by which a person binds himself to perform some act.
SNARE, n. An instrument for catching animals, particularly birds; hence, anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.
scriptures: Proverbs 20:25
It is a snare to the man who devoureth that which is holy, and after vows to make enquiry.
Acts 10:17
Now while Peter doubted in himself what this vision which he had seen should mean, behold, the men which were sent from Cornelius had made enquiry for Simon's house, and stood before the gate,
Ecclesiastes 5:4
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
Acts 10:20
Arise therefore, and get thee down, and go with them, doubting nothing: for I have sent them.
corruption_summary: Commitments are entered on feeling and examined afterward — vows, memberships, marriages, ministries — which is precisely the order Proverbs calls a snare.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 20:25 describes a religious temperament that is now normal: the moment is moving, the commitment is made, and the enquiry begins the following week. A man devoureth that which is holy — makes free with sacred things — and afterwards asks what he has done. Ecclesiastes says the same in plainer terms: when thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it, for he hath no pleasure in fools. The corrective is not to make fewer promises to God out of caution, but to count the cost first, as our Lord taught with the builder and the king going to war, and then to keep what is promised.

Acts 10 supplies the encouraging counterpart, because enquiry is also simply how God's work gets done. Cornelius's men had to ask their way to a tanner's house by the sea, and their arrival at the gate is timed to the minute of Peter's perplexity. The principle to recover is that diligent, unglamorous asking — of Scripture, of elders, of anyone who knows the road — is not weak faith but ordinary obedience, and that God commonly answers the man on the housetop by sending someone who has been making enquiry in the street.
roots_summary: Hebrew baqar (H1239), to seek out, to enquire; neder (H5088), a vow; yaqosh (H3369), to ensnare; Greek dierotao (G1331), to enquire through.
roots_lines: Hebrew baqar (H1239) — to seek, to enquire, to examine; the enquiry made too late.
Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow; what Proverbs says to examine before, not after.
Hebrew yaqosh (H3369) — to lay a snare; what rash consecration becomes.
Hebrew qodesh (H6944) — holiness, a holy thing; that which the rash man devoureth.
Greek dierotao (G1331) — to ask through, to enquire diligently; Cornelius's men at Joppa.
usage: “After vows to make enquiry” — the order that is a snare.
“Had made enquiry for Simon's house, and stood before the gate”.
“Defer not to pay it” — the counsel enquiry should have preceded.

pos: n. (a person unknown or unnamed; a person of consequence)
etymology: From some and body. The Authorized Version uses it twice, and the two uses are opposite: the Lord saying somebody hath touched him, and Theudas boasting himself to be somebody.
biblical_def: In the press around Jesus a woman touched the border of his garment and was healed, and the Lord stopped the crowd: “And Jesus said, Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me” (Luke 8:46). Peter had just objected that the multitude thronged him — many were touching, one had touched, and the Lord distinguished the faith from the crush. He would not let her go away healed and anonymous; he required her to come trembling and declare before all the people why she had touched him, and then sent her in peace. The second use is Gamaliel's: “For before these days rose up Theudas, boasting himself to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered, and brought to nought” (Acts 5:36). To claim to be somebody is the mark of the impostor; to be named by Christ is the portion of the nobody who touched him in faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines somebody as a person unknown or uncertain; a person indeterminate; and also, a person of consideration.
webster_full: SOMEBODY, n. A person unknown or uncertain; a person indeterminate.
SOMEBODY, n. A person of consideration; as, he thinks himself somebody.
THRONG, v.t. To crowd or press, as persons; to oppress or annoy with a crowd of people.
VIRTUE, n. Strength; that substance or quality of physical bodies by which they act and produce effects; efficacy.
BOAST, v.i. To brag or vaunt one's self; to make an ostentatious display of one's own worth or actions.
scriptures: Luke 8:46
And Jesus said, Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me.
Acts 5:36

For before these days rose up Theudas, boasting himself to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered, and brought to nought.
Luke 8:47

And when the woman saw that she was not hid, she came trembling, and falling down before him, she declared unto him before all the people for what cause she had touched him, and how she was healed immediately.
Galatians 6:3
For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.
corruption_summary: The reigning ambition is to be somebody — known, followed, counted — and Scripture attaches that phrase to an impostor whose movement was scattered and brought to nought.
corruption_paragraphs: An age that measures a life by visibility has made being somebody nearly the definition of success, and the church has its own version, in which a ministry that is not known is assumed not to be significant. Acts 5:36 is a cold shower. Theudas boasted himself to be somebody, gathered four hundred men, and the whole thing came to nothing when he died. Paul states the principle without softening it: if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself. The desire to be somebody is not ambition to be disciplined but a lie to be repented of.

Luke 8 gives the alternative, and it is far better than obscurity. The woman was a nobody by every measure the crowd used — unnamed, ceremonially unclean, twelve years poorer and no better — and Christ stopped in the middle of an urgent errand to a synagogue ruler's dying daughter because somebody hath touched me. He would not leave her anonymous. She came trembling, declared before all the people, and went away called Daughter. To be named by Christ is the only somebody worth being, and it is given to those who touch him in faith rather than those who announce themselves.
roots_summary: Greek tis (G5100), someone, a certain one; dunamis (G1411), power or virtue; haptomai (G680), to touch; megas (G3173), great.
roots_lines: Greek tis (G5100) — a certain one, somebody; both the woman and the impostor.
Greek haptomai (G680) — to fasten to, to touch; distinguished from the crowd's thronging.
Greek dunamis (G1411) — power, virtue; that which went out of him at her touch.
Greek ochlos (G3793) — the crowd, the multitude; many pressed, one touched.
Greek thugater (G2364) — daughter; the name Christ gave the woman who was nobody.
usage: “Somebody hath touched me” — faith distinguished from a crowd.
“Boasting himself to be somebody” — and brought to nought.
“She declared unto him before all the people” — no anonymous healing.

pos: a. (not equal; not even or just)
etymology: From un- and equal, Latin aequalis. The word occurs twice in the Authorized Version, both in Ezekiel 18, and both times it is the charge Israel brought against God, thrown back at them.
biblical_def: Ezekiel 18 is the chapter that dismantles the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes and children's teeth set on edge. God insists that the soul that sinneth, it shall die, that a wicked man who turns shall live, and that a righteous man who turns shall die in his sin. Israel's reply is a complaint about fairness, and God answers it twice in identical words: “Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. Hear now, O house of Israel; Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal?” (Ezekiel 18:25), and again, “Yet saith the house of Israel, The way of the Lord is not equal. O house of Israel, are not my ways equal? are not your ways unequal?” (Ezekiel 18:29). The accusation is returned as a question. The chapter ends not in argument but in appeal: cast away from you all your transgressions, make you a new heart and a new spirit, for why will ye die, O house of Israel?
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unequal as not equal; not even; not of the same size, length, breadth or quality; and also, not equitable; not just.
webster_full: UNEQUAL, a. Not equal; not even; not of the same size, length, breadth, quantity or quality.
UNEQUAL, a. Inadequate; insufficient; as, a person unequal to a task.
UNEQUAL, a. Not equitable; not just; partial; as, an unequal decision.
EQUAL, a. Having the same magnitude or dimensions; even; uniform; just; equitable.
IMPARTIAL, a. Not partial; not biased in favor of one party more than another; indifferent; just.
scriptures: Ezekiel 18:25
Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. Hear now, O house of Israel; Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal?
Ezekiel 18:29
Yet saith the house of Israel, The way of the Lord is not equal. O house of Israel, are not my ways equal? are not your ways unequal?
Ezekiel 18:31
Cast away from you all your transgressions, whereby ye have transgressed; and make you a new heart and a new spirit: for why will ye die, O house of Israel?
Ezekiel 18:32
For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye.
corruption_summary: The commonest charge against God is that his ways are unfair, and it is usually made by men applying a standard they do not apply to themselves; Ezekiel answers the charge by turning it around.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection in Ezekiel 18:25 is the oldest one there is, and it is alive in every generation: the way of the Lord is not equal. God does not answer it by explaining his providence in detail. He asks a counter-question — are not your ways unequal? — and repeats it four verses later in case the point was missed. The complaint assumes a standard of fairness, and the standard, wherever the complainer got it, condemns the complainer first. A man who keeps one measure for God's dealings and another for his own is not in a position to arbitrate equity.

What makes the chapter more than a rebuke is where it lands. Having refused the argument, God does not close the door; he opens it: cast away from you all your transgressions, whereby ye have transgressed; and make you a new heart and a new spirit: for why will ye die, O house of Israel? And then, in the next breath, I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth. The God accused of being unequal is the God who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and says so to the people currently accusing him. That is not a defence of his justice so much as a display of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew takan (H8505), to weigh, to make even or equal; derek (H1870), a way; shuwb (H7725), to turn or repent; chaphets (H2654), to delight in.
roots_lines: Hebrew takan (H8505) — to balance, to weigh out, to be equal; the verb in Ezekiel 18:25.
Hebrew derek (H1870) — a road, a way; the ways of God and of the house of Israel compared.
Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, to repent; the hinge of the whole chapter.
Hebrew chaphets (H2654) — to delight in; I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth.
Hebrew leb chadash — a new heart; what God commands and, in Ezekiel 36, promises to give.
usage: “The way of the Lord is not equal” — the oldest accusation.
“Are not your ways unequal?” — the charge returned as a question.
“Why will ye die, O house of Israel?” — where the rebuke lands.

etymology: From weight, Old English gewiht. The Authorized Version uses the adjective twice, once of sand outweighed by a fool's wrath, and once of letters whose weight was conceded by men who despised the writer.
biblical_def: Solomon weighs three things against each other: “A stone is heavy, and the sand weighty; but a fool's wrath is heavier than them both” (Proverbs 27:3). A stone can be set down and sand can be shifted; the fool's anger is the load that cannot be put off by the man who must bear it. The other use is Paul quoting his critics against himself: “For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible” (2 Corinthians 10:10). The Corinthian party granted the weight of what he wrote and dismissed the man who wrote it. Paul's answer is that such as he is in word by letters when absent, such will he be in deed when present — and he refuses throughout the chapter to measure himself by those who commend themselves. Weight in Scripture belongs to the matter and to the God behind it, not to the platform or the presence of the speaker.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines weighty as having great weight; heavy; ponderous; and figuratively, important; momentous; forcible; adapted to turn the balance in the mind.
webster_full: WEIGHTY, a. Having great weight; heavy; ponderous; as, a weighty body.
WEIGHTY, a. Important; momentous; forcible; adapted to turn the balance in the mind, or to convince.
WEIGHTY, a. Rigorous; severe; as, weighty punishment.
PONDEROUS, a. Very heavy; weighty; as, a ponderous shield.
CONTEMPTIBLE, a. Worthy of contempt; despicable; mean; vile.
scriptures: Proverbs 27:3
A stone is heavy, and the sand weighty; but a fool's wrath is heavier than them both.
2 Corinthians 10:10
For his letters, say they, are weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible.
2 Corinthians 10:11
Let such an one think this, that, such as we are in word by letters when we are absent, such will we be also in deed when we are present.
2 Corinthians 10:12

For we dare not make ourselves of the number, or compare ourselves with some that commend themselves: but they measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves among themselves, are not wise.
corruption_summary: Weight is assigned by presence and delivery — how impressive a man seems in the room — and Paul's critics used exactly that measure, conceding the force of his letters while despising his person.
corruption_paragraphs: The Corinthian complaint is strikingly modern: the content is weighty, but the man is unimpressive, and therefore the man may be disregarded. That is the logic of a culture that evaluates by presence, platform and delivery. Paul's reply in the next verse is not a defence of his charisma but a warning — such as we are in word by letters when we are absent, such will we be also in deed when we are present — and then, in verse 12, the diagnosis: they measure themselves by themselves, and compare themselves among themselves, and are not wise.

Proverbs 27:3 gives the other and more personal weight. A fool's wrath is heavier than stone or sand, and anyone who has lived under an angry man knows the arithmetic is exact. Scripture does not tell the sufferer that the load is imaginary. It names it as the heaviest thing in the verse, which is itself a mercy, and elsewhere counsels not making friendship with an angry man lest a man learn his ways. The principle to recover is to weigh matter rather than manner, in the pulpit and in the home: what is said, whether it is true, and whether the one saying it will be in deed what he is in word.
roots_summary: Hebrew nebel (H5192) and koved (H3514), heaviness; kaas (H3708), vexation or wrath; Greek barus (G926), weighty; exoutheneo (G1848), to despise.
roots_lines: Hebrew koved (H3514) — heaviness, weight; the root also behind glory, which is weightiness.
Hebrew kaas (H3708) — vexation, provocation, wrath; the fool's anger heavier than sand.
Hebrew eviyl (H191) — a fool, one perverse and quarrelsome; the bearer of that wrath.
Greek barus (G926) — heavy, weighty, forcible; his letters are weighty and powerful.
Greek exoutheneo (G1848) — to make nothing of, to despise; his speech contemptible.
usage: “A fool's wrath is heavier than them both” — the load that cannot be set down.
“His letters, say they, are weighty and powerful” — the matter conceded.
“They measuring themselves by themselves... are not wise”.

pos: n. (the state of being full of joy; gladness)
etymology: From joy, Old French joie, Latin gaudium. The Authorized Version uses the noun twice, and they are among the most searching verses in Scripture: joyfulness as the thing Israel failed to serve with, and joyfulness as the fruit of being strengthened for patience.
biblical_def: In the long catalogue of curses, Moses states the cause of them in a single verse that has nothing to do with outward failure: “Because thou servedst not the LORD thy God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things” (Deuteronomy 28:47). The service was rendered; what was missing was the joy in rendering it, and that — in a season of abundance — is named as the reason judgment came. Paul prays for the Colossians in terms that sound, until the last word, like a prayer for endurance: “Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness” (Colossians 1:11). All might and glorious power are asked for, and what they produce is patience, longsuffering, and joy in the middle of both. Divine strength in the New Testament is not usually given so that the load may be lifted, but so that it may be carried gladly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines joyfulness as gladness; joy; and the state of being full of joy or delight.
webster_full: JOYFULNESS, n. Gladness; joy; the state of being joyful.
JOYFUL, a. Full of joy; very glad; exulting; as, the heart is joyful.
GLADNESS, n. Joy, or a moderate degree of joy and exhilaration; pleasure of mind.
LONGSUFFERING, a. Bearing injuries or provocation for a long time; patient; not easily provoked.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring or fretfulness.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 28:47
Because thou servedst not the LORD thy God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things;
Colossians 1:11
Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness;
Deuteronomy 28:48

Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies which the LORD shall send against thee, in hunger, and in thirst, and in nakedness, and in want of all things: and he shall put a yoke of iron upon thy neck, until he have destroyed thee.
Nehemiah 8:10

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
corruption_summary: Joy is treated as a temperament some have and others do not, or as an emotion to be manufactured; Scripture commands it, makes its absence a ground of judgment, and supplies it by God's own power.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 28:47 is one of the most alarming verses in the Bible for respectable religion. The people served. They kept a form. What God names as the reason for the curses that follow is that they did not serve with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, and that in a time of the abundance of all things. Duty performed without delight is not a lesser obedience God will accept as second best; here it is the charge. That cuts directly against the common assumption that joy is optional decoration on the real business of faithfulness.

Colossians 1:11 keeps this from becoming a counsel of despair or a demand for manufactured cheerfulness. Paul does not tell the Colossians to try harder to be joyful; he prays that they would be strengthened with all might according to God's glorious power, and he names joyfulness as part of what that power produces, alongside patience and longsuffering. Nehemiah gives the same order in a sentence: the joy of the LORD is your strength. Joy is a fruit, sought in prayer and given by God, and it is possible under a load rather than only after it is lifted.
roots_summary: Hebrew simchah (H8057), gladness, joy; tuwb lebab, gladness of heart; Greek chara (G5479), joy; makrothumia (G3115), longsuffering.
roots_lines: Hebrew simchah (H8057) — joy, gladness, mirth; the joyfulness of Deuteronomy 28:47.
Hebrew tuwb lebab — goodness of heart; the AV's gladness of heart in the same verse.
Hebrew chedvah (H2304) — joy, gladness; the joy of the LORD is your strength.
Greek chara (G5479) — joy, delight; the last word of Paul's prayer in Colossians 1:11.
Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, patient endurance; joy's companion under a load.
usage: “Because thou servedst not the LORD thy God with joyfulness” — the charge.
“Unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness” — what power produces.
“The joy of the LORD is your strength” — not the reward of it.

etymology: From plow, Old English ploh, and men. The Authorized Version uses the plural twice, and the two verses stand at opposite ends of hope: plowmen ashamed in a drought, and strangers serving as plowmen to a restored people.
biblical_def: Jeremiah paints a drought with a single image of shame: “Because the ground is chapt, for there was no rain in the earth, the plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads” (Jeremiah 14:4). Men whose whole skill is in the soil stand over cracked ground with nothing to do and hide their faces — the passage goes on to the hind calving in the field and forsaking her young. Isaiah's restoration promise turns the picture over: “And strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and the sons of the alien shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers” (Isaiah 61:5). The chapter is the one our Lord read at Nazareth, and the verse describes a reversal so complete that the nations who had oppressed Israel come to serve in her fields. Between the two verses lies the whole of covenant history: the rain withheld in judgment, and the ground worked again in mercy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a plowman as one who plows or holds a plow; a cultivator of the earth; and figuratively, a rustic or countryman.
webster_full: PLOWMAN, n. One that plows or holds a plow; a cultivator of the earth.
PLOWMAN, n. A countryman; a rustic; a hardy laborer.
PLOW, n. An instrument for turning up, breaking and preparing the ground for receiving the seed.
VINEDRESSER, n. One who dresses, trims, prunes and cultivates vines.
CHAPT, a. Cracked; opened in long slits, as the ground in a drought.
scriptures: Jeremiah 14:4
Because the ground is chapt, for there was no rain in the earth, the plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads.
Isaiah 61:5
And strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and the sons of the alien shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers.
Jeremiah 14:3

And their nobles have sent their little ones to the waters: they came to the pits, and found no water; they returned with their vessels empty; they were ashamed and confounded, and covered their heads.
Isaiah 61:1

The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
corruption_summary: Agricultural labour is treated as unskilled and forgettable, where Scripture makes plowmen the barometer of a nation under God — ashamed in judgment, and served by strangers in mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misjudgment is the contempt an urban society develops for the work that feeds it. Scripture measures the state of a nation by what its plowmen are doing. Jeremiah 14 does not announce the drought by economic statistics; it shows men who know one trade standing over chapt ground with their heads covered, and nobles sending their little ones to pits that have no water. Shame is the word chosen, because a man who cannot work his ground feels the failure in his person.

Isaiah 61 supplies the hope and the frame. The chapter opens with the Spirit of the Lord GOD upon the Anointed to preach good tidings unto the meek and to bind up the brokenhearted — the passage our Lord read in the synagogue at Nazareth and declared fulfilled in their ears. The plowmen verse is part of what that gospel brings: a people so restored that the sons of the alien work their fields. The principle to recover is that honest work in the ground is not beneath the covenant but inside it, and that the same Christ who binds up the brokenhearted intends the ground itself to be blessed.
roots_summary: Hebrew ikkar (H406), a plowman or husbandman; charash (H2790), to plow or engrave; bosh (H954), to be ashamed; nekar (H5236), a foreigner.
roots_lines: Hebrew ikkar (H406) — a plowman, a husbandman; the word in both Isaiah 61:5 and Jeremiah 14:4.
Hebrew charash (H2790) — to cut in, to plow, to engrave; the labour itself.
Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, confounded; the plowmen covered their heads.
Hebrew nekar (H5236) — that which is foreign; the sons of the alien who shall serve.
Hebrew koreem (H3755) — vinedressers; paired with plowmen in the restoration.
usage: “The plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads” — a drought made visible.
“The sons of the alien shall be your plowmen” — the reversal in mercy.
“Because the ground is chapt” — judgment written in the soil.

etymology: Old French norrir, from Latin nutrire, to feed. The noun occurs once in the Authorized Version, in the blessing the women of Bethlehem pronounce over Naomi at the end of Ruth, and it is one of the sweetest titles in Scripture.
biblical_def: The book of Ruth ends with the women speaking to Naomi about a newborn: “And he shall be unto thee a restorer of thy life, and a nourisher of thine old age: for thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons, hath born him” (Ruth 4:15). Naomi had come home from Moab saying call me not Naomi, call me Mara, for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me — empty, she said, when the LORD hath brought me home again. The child Obed answers that emptiness: a restorer of life and a nourisher of old age. The verse also settles the worth of Ruth, a Moabitess, in terms no Israelite would use lightly — better to thee than seven sons. Obed became the father of Jesse, the father of David; the nourisher of one old woman's age stands in the genealogy of Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nourish as to feed and cause to grow; to supply with matter which increases bulk or supplies waste; to support; to maintain.
webster_full: NOURISH, v.t. To feed and cause to grow; to supply a living or organized body with matter which increases its bulk.
NOURISH, v.t. To support; to maintain by feeding; as, a father nourishes his children.
NOURISH, v.t. To cherish; to comfort; to encourage; as, to nourish hope.
NOURISHER, n. One that nourishes; that which nourishes or sustains.
RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former good state; to repair; to recover; to bring back.
scriptures: Ruth 4:15
And he shall be unto thee a restorer of thy life, and a nourisher of thine old age: for thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons, hath born him. a nourisher
Ruth 1:20
And she said unto them, Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me. Naomi: that is, Pleasant Mara: that is, Bitter
Ruth 1:21
I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty: why then call ye me Naomi, seeing the LORD hath testified against me, and the Almighty hath afflicted me?
Ruth 4:17
And the women her neighbours gave it a name, saying, There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David.
corruption_summary: Old age is widely regarded as a burden to be managed by institutions, where Ruth ends with a family charged to be the nourisher of an old woman's years and a foreign daughter in law reckoned better than seven sons.
corruption_paragraphs: The arrangement most societies now default to is that the care of the aged is outsourced, and the family's role shrinks to visiting. Ruth 4:15 assumes something else entirely: the child born into the house is a nourisher of thine old age, and the whole book has been about a younger woman refusing to leave an older one — whither thou goest, I will go. Paul states the same duty as a test of faith: if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith and is worse than an infidel. The nourishing of the old is not a sentimental extra but a mark of the household of God.

The second thing to recover is what the verse says about Ruth. A Moabitess, from a people Israel had reason to despise, is reckoned by the women of Bethlehem as better to thee than seven sons — the highest comparison their language had. Naomi went out full and came home empty by her own account, and God answered the emptiness with a foreign daughter, a kinsman redeemer, and a child in her lap whose grandson would be David. The nourisher of an old woman's age turns out to be a link in the line of the Messiah.
roots_summary: Hebrew kuwl (H3557), to sustain or nourish; shuwb (H7725), to restore; seybah (H7872), grey hair, old age; goel (H1350), a kinsman redeemer.
roots_lines: Hebrew kuwl (H3557) — to contain, to sustain, to nourish; a nourisher of thine old age.
Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, to restore; a restorer of thy life.
Hebrew seybah (H7872) — grey-headedness, old age; the season this child would feed.
Hebrew goel (H1350) — a kinsman redeemer; Boaz's office, and the type of Christ.
Hebrew Mara (H4755) — bitter; the name Naomi asked for, and God overruled.
usage: “A restorer of thy life, and a nourisher of thine old age”.
“Better to thee than seven sons” — said of a Moabitess.
“Call me Mara” — the name the last chapter answers.
